cases.name: Kennedy Space Center, Launch Complex 39
cases.meta: Merritt Island, Florida · built 1962–67 · NASA and its contractors
cases.theory: The complex follows the engineering logic Pascoe finds in the first airfields, which "only occupied itself with the needs of the aircraft, not with those of the passengers" (p. 27). NASA’s life-support baseline reads the crew the same way, as an interface that "accounts for all metabolic inputs and outputs from crew members" (Ewert et al. 2022). The vehicle is the client; the crew is one of its systems.
cases.method: Rockets are stacked upright in the Vehicle Assembly Building and carried 3 to 4 miles to the pad at walking pace. The crew is quartered and suited in the Operations and Checkout Building, driven to the pad, and crosses the crew access arm to the hatch. Spectators are held at the press site, 3 miles from Pad 39A.
cases.outcome: Every station of a rite of passage is there: seclusion, dressing, a procession, a threshold. None of it was designed as one. The breakfast, the walkout past the cameras and the Astrovan grew up around a plan drawn for the vehicle.
cases.take: The launch complex already holds a rite of passage. It has never been given an architecture.
cases.src: Benson and Faherty 1978; Ewert, Chen and Powell 2022; Pascoe 2001, p. 27; Wikipedia, “Launch Complex 39” and “Launch Complex 39 Press Site”

cases.name: Baikonur: the cosmonauts’ rituals
cases.theory: Traditions are often recent and invented (Hobsbawm and Ranger 1983). At Baikonur they were invented around a single day, Gagarin’s, and have been repeated ever since (Gerovitch 2015).
cases.method: Nobody designed it. Each crew repeats Gagarin’s day: flowers at the Kremlin wall, a tree planted in the cosmonauts’ grove, a haircut, the film White Sun of the Desert the night before, the hotel room door signed on the morning of launch, a priest’s blessing (added in 1994), and a stop on the road to the pad, where the bus’s rear wheel is wetted as Gagarin did.
cases.outcome: One of the densest departure rituals in the world lives in a hotel, a road, a grove and a pad used for more than sixty years. Repetition has made it stronger, not emptier.
cases.take: Meaning can live in practice with almost no designed place, and routine can carry it. Architecture has to make room for rites, not replace them.
cases.src: Gerovitch 2015; Hobsbawm and Ranger 1983; Space.com 2018; Atlas Obscura

cases.name: Babylon: the Processional Street and the Ishtar Gate
cases.meta: Babylon · c. 575 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II · rebuilt in Berlin by Walter Andrae, 1930
imgs: The Ishtar Gate’s lions, Pergamon Museum
The Processional Street at Babylon today, walls rebuilt
cases.theory: For Andrae, who rebuilt it in Berlin, the route was "a Babylonian path of initiation" (Böhme, p. 216), meant to purify everyone heading into the holy city (p. 228).
cases.method: A walled street more than half a mile long, lined with over 120 glazed lions, runs from the New Year festival house outside the walls, through the Ishtar Gate with its dragons and bulls, to the temple of Marduk. The walker meets lion, bull and dragon one after another (p. 230), and sight along the route was graded by rank.
cases.outcome: The city’s most important rite was given a permanent route. The architecture does the transforming: the walker is prepared by length, repetition and a single threshold.
cases.take: A departure can be designed as a sequence that ends in a threshold. This is exactly what the walkout at Kennedy lacks.
cases.src: Böhme, pp. 216–230 (quoting Andrae); World History Encyclopedia, “Ishtar Gate”; photograph: Madain Project

cases.name: Ise Jingu: the rebuilding every twenty years
cases.meta: Ise, Japan · since c. 690 · the 62nd rebuilding in 2013, the 63rd under way
imgs: Old and new sites, side by side
Okihiki: the public hauls the timber
cases.theory: Renewal rather than permanence. The form is kept by rebuilding it, and the real product of each rebuilding is the handing-down of skills (Adams 1998, pp. 49–56). Kawazoe read Ise as a design with "its own metabolism" (Reynolds 2001, p. 331).
cases.method: The shrine buildings are rebuilt on an adjacent plot every twenty years; the old ones are then taken down and their timber reused at other shrines. Some thirty rites mark the work over several years, and in the Okihiki, residents and visitors haul the new timber to the shrine themselves.
cases.outcome: The shrine is about 1,300 years old, and its buildings are never more than twenty. The work is public, repeated and handed down, and the work is the rite.
cases.take: Preparation becomes ritual when the work is visible, shared and handed down.
cases.src: Adams 1998, pp. 49–56; Reynolds 2001, p. 331; Visit Iseshima, “Shikinen Sengu”

cases.name: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
cases.meta: Washington, D.C. · 1982 · Maya Lin, chosen from 1,421 competition entries
imgs: Space Mirror Memorial, Kennedy Visitor Complex, 1991
cases.theory: A memorial that asks the visitor to face the loss rather than celebrate a victory. Lin described "a rift in the earth," where "it is up to each individual to resolve or come to terms with this loss."
cases.method: Two black granite walls, each 246 feet long, are cut into the ground and meet at an angle. They list more than 58,000 names in the order they died, starting and ending at the vertex, so the war’s beginning and end meet. The polished stone reflects the visitor among the names.
cases.outcome: Visitors became witnesses: they read, trace and leave things, and the Park Service keeps what they leave. Kennedy’s Space Mirror Memorial (1991), with the names of the astronauts who died, follows the same idea.
cases.take: Architecture can give an honest account of risk and loss, and turn spectators into witnesses.
cases.src: Lin, competition statement, 1981, via the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund; Wikipedia, “Vietnam Veterans Memorial” and “Space Mirror Memorial”

cases.name: From the TWA Flight Center to Roissy
cases.meta: New York, 1962, Eero Saarinen · Paris, 1974, Paul Andreu
cases.theory: Gordon and Pascoe trace the airport from romance to processing. Augé opens Non-Places with a traveller passing through Roissy (pp. 1–5). Saarinen wanted TWA to "express the drama and specialness and excitement of travel."
cases.method: TWA: a thin concrete shell over one open hall, with views out to the runway and tubes leading to the gates. Roissy: a ten-storey concrete drum, glass tubes of escalators crossing its core, and passages out to seven satellites. The plane is out of sight.
cases.outcome: TWA’s views were later closed off for "circulation, process, containment" (Pascoe, p. 201). It could not take jumbo jets or modern security, closed in 2001, and is now a hotel. Twelve years separate the two buildings.
cases.take: Routine turns the departure hall from an experience into a process within a generation, unless the meaning is given a place somewhere else.
cases.src: Pascoe 2001, pp. 200–201; Augé 1995, pp. 1–5; Gordon 2004; Britannica, “Terminal 1”; Wikipedia, “TWA Flight Center”

cases.name: Spaceport America
cases.meta: New Mexico · completed 2011 · Foster + Partners, for Virgin Galactic and the State of New Mexico
imgs: The Gateway, the terminal and hangar
The approach: the road into the channel
cases.theory: The first spaceport built for paying passengers rather than state astronauts: the airport’s terminal brought to the departure from Earth, with the approach designed as a journey.
cases.method: The building is dug into the desert. Visitors and astronauts arrive through “a deep channel cut into the landscape”, whose “retaining walls form an exhibition space” on the history of space exploration and of the region. The hangar sits at the centre, administration to one side, flight training and preparation to the other, with full-height glass onto the runway.
cases.outcome: A designed route for the one leaving and a view for the ones watching, in one building. The first commercial flight left only in June 2023, twelve years after it opened: the routine it was built for is still arriving.
cases.take: Routine departure can still be given a route: a way in through the land and its history, ending at the runway.
cases.src: Foster + Partners project text, via Dezeen, 2011; Virgin Galactic, 2023; photographs: Land Rover MENA (CC BY 2.0); Forbes, 2021

framework.sub: The map from the first sheet, read: the whole study faded behind, the seven case studies placed on it, and what it adds up to along the base.
text: This is the map from the first sheet, faded: the study’s 409 terms and events across four layers, eight eras and a projected future. Over it sit the seven case studies, each placed in the layers where it holds the meaning of departure, at the time it was made, and marked hollow where it holds that meaning back.

Read against the whole study, the two findings along the base hold. Before the heroic age, the forms on the map carry the rite: the seclusion lodge, the processional way, the pilgrim road, the quay. From it, form goes to the machine, as Pascoe, Gordon and Augé trace for the airport, and the meaning survives in the practices and the testimony around it.

The cases show the same movement up close. In the oldest, form carries the rite: the route at Babylon, the rebuilt shrine at Ise. In the modern ones, the meaning survives in ritual repeated every launch (Baikonur, Kennedy) and in testimony to the risk (the Vietnam Veterans Memorial and Kennedy’s Space Mirror), while the one building made for the departure itself became a process within a generation (TWA to Roissy). The newest, Spaceport America, stages the departure as a route again.
framework.position: Routine does not empty departure of meaning. It moves it from the one leaving to the witness and the preparer, and from the event to ritual and testimony. At the launch complex, form went to the vehicle; neither ritual nor testimony has been given a place.
framework.proposition: If the launch complex gives form to the practices and the honest account that routine leaves behind, rather than to the event itself, departure can stay meaningful as it becomes ordinary.

discussion.TITLE: Discussion
discussion.SUB: The position, turned into a design problem: routine is not one pace.
discussion.C1_P1: The position says that routine moves the meaning of departure from the event to ritual and testimony. The discussion adds one thing: routine is not one pace. Leaving the Earth becomes several rhythms at once, and each carries the meaning differently.
RHY: the launch as work. Only the preparers are there.
the crew change, the servicing run. A rite: the same day repeated, as at Baikonur.
the long mission. Still an event: the crowd comes, and the witness matters.
C2_P: The three rhythms are not a forecast. They are already here, and they are moving apart. In 2025 there were 324 orbital launches, one every 27 hours. Eight of them carried people: fewer than in 1985, and never more than eleven in any year since 1961. Nine crews left Earth orbit between 1968 and 1972, then none for fifty-three years, until Artemis II in April 2026.

Who launches has changed as much as how often. Fifteen countries have put their own rocket into orbit in sixty-nine years. Twenty-two companies founded to do it have done it too, all but three of them since 2017. The next complex will not be one nation’s gate.

So the launch became routine; the human departure did not; and the rare one has just come back. One complex has to hold all three at the same time, for many parties. That is the design problem, and it is stated before a site or a form. How many rhythms there are, and how they meet, is left open.
C3: Not chosen. The test that matters comes from the rhythms: a place with launches already there, or coming, and room for all three. The candidates are on the image board: Starbase, a purpose-built spaceport, Kennedy’s heroic fabric.
discussion.SRC: Data: Space Stats Online, spacestatsonline.com, orbital launches only, updated 30 August 2026; NASA, 1 April 2026. Suborbital flights are not counted. Countries: their own rocket to orbit, attempts counted, Europe as one. Companies: firms founded to launch, not the state contractors, with an orbital attempt of their own rocket; own count from the same rocket list.
NOTE: A launch is routine now. A departure is not yet.
The complex was built for the first. This thesis builds for the second.
